Briser le silence d’un génocide oublié: Breaking the silence of a forgotten genocide
« Lorsqu’elle m’a partagé son expérience: “When she shared her experience with me, I realized that her story is the story of my ancestors – it hadn’t hit me before.”
Le 27 janvier dernier, alors qu’on céléb: Last January 27, as International Holocaust Remembrance Day was being observed, the European Roma Rights Centre shared testimonies from Roma around the world who had answered one very simple question: “What is your story about the Roma genocide?”
En lisant ces témoignages, je me suis ap: As I read these testimonies, I realized I didn’t know enough about my own history. When I was little, my paternal grandmother told me that the Nazis had come to her village in Serbia and shaved her head, because they said Roma were dirty and had lice. I was only eight at the time, and I didn’t ask her any more questions. So that is all I knew, before January 27, about my family’s history during the Holocaust.
Cette nuit-là, après avoir lu plusieurs: That night, after reading several testimonies, I started searching databases for the names of people held in concentration camps in the former Yugoslavia. I found my grandmother’s name, but the date of birth didn’t match. I asked my uncle: “How is it that the Nazis shaved her head? Was she imprisoned?” According to him, she hadn’t been. He explained that the officers had come to the village to imprison the Roma, but when they saw my great-grandfather’s kindness, they spared his family.
Un officier avait toutefois décidé de ra: One officer had nevertheless decided to shave the head of one of his six daughters – my grandmother Radmila – who had long black hair. My grandmother, like many Roma women, had hair down to her hips until the very end of her life. Today, I better understand why it was so dear to her. The next day, I talk about it with my mother and she tells me flatly: “My grandfather was imprisoned too, the whole family was back then, I don’t remember if my father was.”
Je ne connais pas encore le reste de ces: I don’t yet know the rest of these stories; my grandparents have all died. Traditionally, among the Roma, we don’t talk about death, and very rarely about our misfortunes. We have a saying: “The dead with the dead, and the living with the living.” At 85, Lajos Molnar is breaking the silence. Accompanied by his 11-year-old granddaughter and his daughter Kristin, he tells us about his experience. He wanted his granddaughter to be there. “She’s old enough now, she needs to know,” he told Kristin before the interview. Mr. Molnar was born in Budapest, Hungary. When the war began, he was five. “From 1941 on, I remember everything, every second of the war,” he tells us in the garden of his home in Montréal. He, too, had his head shaved during the war. “I was completely bald, the Nazis said we were dirty and full of lice. We had to shave our heads; it was so they could recognize us,” he explains.
Au début de la guerre, le père de M. Mol: At the start of the war, Mr. Molnar’s father was in the Hungarian army in Russia. He returned to Hungary in 1943. Six months later, the militias came to take him to a concentration camp, because he was Roma. “When they needed us for the army, we were Hungarians, but after that, it was over, we were Gypsies,” he says. Four months later, the father managed to escape from the ghetto and came back to the village. “That very night, at 2 or 3 in the morning, the militia comes to our place and says: ‘We’re looking for Mr. Molnar; he escaped from the ghetto.’ My father hid under the feather mattress on the bed. I lay down on the bed, and they didn’t see him. We were lucky they didn’t have a dog with them, because if they had found him, we would all have been gunned down in the yard,” recalls the man in his eighties. The next day, the entire family left the village of Cinkota for Budapest. “We all took refuge in an empty house in Budapest.
À un moment donné, il y avait des bombar: At one point, there were bombings, and we all hid in the cellar. We were there in the cellar, doing nothing, just waiting for death,” Mr. Molnar explains.
« Un jour, des milices sont venues nous: “One day, militias came for us. Someone had turned us in. There were nearly 200 of us in the cellar. They took us out around 3 or 4 in the morning and lined us up against the wall to kill us. My father was the last one out of the building. Suddenly, the officer recognized my father and said: ‘Lajos, I have to kill you; no, that’s not true, we’re leaving.’ He had recognized my father, who, before the war, had played with his orchestra in an officers’ club.” Music saved the Molnar family more than once. In the spring of 1945, before the end of the war, the Russians were coming to find Germans in the houses of Budapest. For the Molnars, the Russians were as terrifying as the Germans, since many Russian officers raped Roma women.
« Mon père, parce qu’il connaissait l’ar: “My father, because he knew the Russian army, explained to me: ‘When you hear the sound of boots in the hallway coming toward the cellar, you go to the door, and when you see a soldier, you take out your violin and start playing Russian dances.’ One day, an officer opened the cellar door in Budapest, and I started to play. He took off his machine gun and started to dance. He was looking for Germans and shouted: ‘Nemski, nemski!’ I will never forget that stocky little man.”
Peu après, la famille retourna à Cinkota: Soon after, the family went back to Cinkota. But fear still gripped the family because of the rape of Roma women by Russian forces. To protect them, he played Russian music on his violin, accompanied by his grandfather on the cello, whenever a Russian soldier approached the family home. “That’s how we saved our mother, our aunts, the women. Every time a car stopped, we played,” Mr. Molnar confides. His aunt and cousin were not as lucky. They were imprisoned in Auschwitz. “We didn’t know what had happened to them. My cousin was raped over and over, she practically lost her mind,” he remembers. The women did survive, however.
Kristin Molnar, la fille de Lajos, a gra: Kristin Molnar, Lajos’s daughter, grew up in Montréal. She first heard about the Holocaust around age eight, in books. When she got to high school, she came across a series of books on the subject, but they said very little about the Roma. “I would read that, and it physically hurt,” she explains. Around age 16, one day while watching a documentary on the Holocaust, she collapses. “My legs gave out, I was in pain and I started to cry,” she recalls. The subject of the Second World War is not often brought up by her father, who told her about his experience in bits and pieces.
C’est lors de notre rencontre qu’elle en: It is during our meeting that she hears the whole story in chronological order for the first time. She still sees its scars in her daily life. “I remember one summer, a few years ago, when I asked him to go get some chairs in the cellar. He said to me: ‘Listen, sweetheart, I can’t go down into a cellar, I’m afraid,’” she says.
« En Hongrie, dans ma famille et dans to: “In Hungary, in my family and throughout the Roma community, we never talk about this. It’s just one more humiliating thing,” she adds. Andras (not his real name) is 18. He is from Miskolc, Hungary, where he experienced racial segregation and neo-Nazi attacks. He doesn’t want to give his real name because he fears attacks from Hungarian neo-Nazis living in Canada. He learned about his family’s story during the Porajmos only about three years ago here, during a presentation at his high school in Toronto, where he has lived since 2016. “Here, the community commemorates the Roma Holocaust every year,” he explains.
J’ai donc décidé d’en faire une présenta: So I decided to do a presentation on it and I started to take an interest in my family’s history.” After a few calls to his aunts in Hungary, he learned that his family had been victims of the Holocaust. “My great-great-uncle and my great-great-aunt were imprisoned in Auschwitz. They never came back. During the war, my great-grandmother was raped by Russian soldiers in our village.”
Il aimerait maintenant que cette histoir: He now wants this story to be passed down from generation to generation in his family. “We have to talk about it, because there is still denial. It’s a history that is still little known, that is absent from our history classes. We have to keep talking about it until we are respected, because our history and our suffering are still being denied,” he exclaims. Andras sees similarities between the stories his aunts told and what he has lived through and what the Roma in Europe are going through. “When I was four, neo-Nazis came to my village to attack the Roma.
Ils ont encerclé ma maison – je me rappe: They surrounded my house – I still remember how I cried, I was afraid of dying, I was afraid my parents would be killed. It’s not normal to go through that in a country that is a member of the European Union,” he says. These events have led many young people to learn about the Second World War.
« Plusieurs jeunes de Miskolc ont commen: “Many young people in Miskolc started to take an interest in this part of our history because of today’s racism,” he reports. Roma journalist and artist Gilda Horvath, who lives in Austria, shares this observation. According to her, the annual commemoration at Auschwitz, where many young Roma gather every August 2, puts into perspective their daily lives, which are still filled with hatred. “It is important to include us in history’s blind spots,” she argues. Ms. Horvath’s great-aunt, Ceija Stojka, was an Auschwitz survivor who campaigned for years for recognition of the Roma Holocaust.
Cette dernière a réalisé de nombreuses p: She created numerous paintings about the Holocaust. Today, Ms. Horvath honours her in museums across Europe and organizes commemoration events. “When she shared her experience with me, I realized that her story is the story of my ancestors – it hadn’t hit me before,” she explains.
Pour Elena Catalina Gauthier, une Rom de: For Elena Catalina Gauthier, a Roma woman from Romania who was adopted by a Québécois couple as a child, learning about the history of the Roma during the Second World War helped her better understand her own journey. Today, she lives in Rimouski and is discovering her origins through reading. For the past three months, the woman in her thirties has been learning about the Roma genocide during the Second World War.
Ayant grandi en région, tout ce qu’elle: Having grown up outside the big cities, everything she knew about her people was negative and full of stereotypes. “Let’s be clear, growing up, being Roma didn’t mean much to me. It was frowned upon, even in my family,” she says. So she never heard of the Roma as victims of the Second World War.
« On ne m’a jamais parlé du fait qu’on l: “No one ever told me they were marked with a T or a Z, that they were locked up in concentration camps. There’s a whole part of history that I didn’t know. Reading this history allowed me to reconnect with my origins, to understand that the Roma are a nation,” she confides. Back in Lajos’s garden, with his daughter and granddaughter, the survivor tells us how his experiences affected his self-esteem.
« J’avais le sentiment d’être une pourri: “I felt like I was scum, like I couldn’t accept being who I am,” he says, thinking back to the years when he was ashamed of his Roma identity. He would like this terrible chapter of Roma history, which is often overshadowed by the dominant narrative of the Second World War, to be officially recognized.
Il souhaite aussi qu’on se souvienne du: He also wants the positive to be remembered: “There were people who defended us all the same, we must not forget that – I had friends,” he recalls, breaking into tears. “People say we’re going to eradicate racism, but we’ll never be able to, because racism is not knowing other people. What hurts me is that my children still have to live through this.” — Lajos Molnar
